draft.title: Hyperbole and oxymoron
card: Hyperbole
deliberate exaggeration for effect. The writer does not mean it literally, and the reader knows it. For example, "I've told you a million times."
Effect of hyperbole
It stresses a strong feeling, such as anger, excitement or embarrassment. It can also make a reader smile.
Oxymoron
two opposite words joined together, such as deafening silence or bittersweet. The two words seem to clash.
Effect of oxymoron
It captures a mixed or hard to name feeling, where two opposite ideas are true at once.
draft.remember: Hyperbole stretches the truth to stress a feeling. An oxymoron joins opposites to capture a mixed feeling.

opts: I was so hungry I could eat a whole horse
The soup was as hot as a furnace
The kitchen was a noisy zoo
The old fridge hummed a sleepy tune
a.why: Eating a whole horse is a deliberate exaggeration that nobody takes literally. The furnace line compares using as, so it is a simile. The zoo line says one thing is another, so it is a metaphor.
a.clue: Which one stretches the truth far past what could happen?

b.q: Leo finishes a hard race and says, "It was a painful joy." Which technique is this, and what does it show?
opts: Oxymoron, showing he felt pain and joy together
Oxymoron, showing the race was exaggerated
Hyperbole, showing he felt pain and joy together
Hyperbole, showing the race was exaggerated
b.why: Painful and joy are opposites joined together, so this is an oxymoron. It captures a mixed feeling that is hard to name. Hyperbole would stretch the truth to stress a feeling, and nothing here is exaggerated.
b.clue: Look at whether the two words clash or whether something is stretched.

a.best: I was so hungry I could eat a whole horse
also_right: The soup was as hot as a furnace

b.best: Oxymoron, showing he felt pain and joy together

problems.detail: 'The soup was as hot as a furnace' is also a deliberate exaggeration: soup cannot be as hot as a furnace. Many teachers would call it a hyperbolic simile, so it is a defensible second answer. The clue 'stretches the truth far past what could happen' fits it too.

The why says the furnace line is a simile and so not hyperbole. This teaches that a line cannot be both, which is false. It also explains simile and metaphor, which belong to point 1, instead of only mentioning them.
The right option is clearly the longest, and it is the only first-person 'so... I could' construction. A student could pick it without knowing the idea.

opts: My school bag weighs a tonne today
My school bag feels very heavy today
My school bag is an awful delight
My school bag holds five heavy books
a.why: A school bag cannot really weigh a tonne, so this is a deliberate exaggeration to stress how heavy it feels. An awful delight joins two opposite words, so it is an oxymoron, not an exaggeration. The other two sentences could simply be true.
